name: PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Karya Pacific Energy — the ramp is the contract's, the price is the market's
frontmatter.summary: IATA trades at Rp71 against our Rp110 target — BUY, 55.4% expected return; base case Rp121. The licence bridge moves to one-half of the mining-property net book. The engine's deck-shock defect biases both shock branches down, so the corrected target is about a quarter higher; the price implies a Newcastle benchmark about a tenth below our path.
thesis: The shares are below our value after the third-quarter report: nine-month net profit attributable was US$1.0m against US$7.2m a year earlier, on flat revenue, a US$2.4m exchange loss and US$4.1m of finance costs [S16, S17]. The operating ramp is intact on the nine months' revenue and the signed KPP contract, so we cut neither volume nor price.

The ramp is real — a five-year KPP Mining contract and 298 Mt of reserves support a move toward 5.3 Mt — but the cash economics are thin: on US$21.1m of EBITDA, US$5.2m of capex, tax and working capital leave US$10.3m of FCFF.

The product is low-calorie thermal coal priced off HBA III [S8], not the 6,000 kcal Newcastle benchmark; the company's own 2026 estimate of 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t is below the 2025 average of 36.5 USD/t [S8 p.86].
Liquidity is tight: nine-month cash fell to US$1.5m while inventories rose to US$37.5m, factoring liabilities to US$8.1m, and current liabilities topped current assets [S16, S17].

blocks.text: **BUY, target Rp110, 55.4% expected return.** The base value is Rp121 and the raw DCF Rp118 against a price of Rp71 [S0]. This revision changes one number and corrects the text around it. The number is the licence bridge: the three non-operating IUP-OPs are carried at one-half — three of six permits — of the US$77.5m mining-property and exploration net book [S12 p.14, Note 11], not the one-third the previous draft used against its own stated count. That line is the whole of the input change but not the whole of the arithmetic: it is the bulk of the move to Rp110, and about one rupiah of the raw value — slightly less on the target — is a re-mark rather than an input. The rupiah translation from the previous version's deck spot to today's accounts for most of that rupiah; the balance is a sub-rupee difference between the two builds that the archive cannot bisect, because the previous run was not kept. Both are disclosed in valuation.restatement_bridge, not absorbed. The engine's deck-shock defect biases both shock branches down, so on a corrected run the target is about a quarter higher and the return near ninety per cent; the valuation section sets the corrected set out in full and the published target stays the engine's lawful build, because no coverage role may edit the engine.

The variant view is that IATA's cash conversion is weaker than the P&L suggests, so the equity is worth the discounted residue of a finite life of tonnes rather than a growth multiple. In FY2025 US$7.6m of net profit came with only US$3.2m of operating cash flow against US$25.2m of capex, and on the plan US$21.1m of EBITDA leaves US$10.3m of FCFF after capex, tax and working capital [S12, S8].

What moves the value is narrow. First, the low-calorie price: the company's own HBA III estimate for 2026 is 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t, below the 2025 average of 36.5 USD/t [S8 p.86]. The November print of 46.6 USD/t is up 2.4% on the prior fortnight and above both, but it is a spot mark without a forward path: cycle position, valued only in the bull [S20]. Second, the RKAB quota: only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial 2026 quota and the H1 decline was attributed to it [S6, S8, S5]; nine-month revenue implies the mid-year revision was delivered for 2026, so the live risk is whether it rolls into 2027.

The gap to our value is open. At Rp71 the shares trade on 12.4x EV/EBITDA and 24.5x P/E on trough FY2026E earnings, but 8.4x and 14.0x on the FY2027E ramp year the DCF values [S0]. The reverse DCF, solved on a clean deck series, finds the price consistent with an FY2027E Newcastle benchmark about a tenth BELOW our US$118/t [deck]: the market is discounting coal as well as tonnes and confidence. The engine's own solver prints that benchmark above our path only because it runs through the broken shock path described in the valuation section, so we state the direction the clean solve shows, not its root.

PT Karya Pacific Energy Tbk is an IDX-listed coal miner, formerly PT MNC Energy Investments Tbk [S12 Note 1]. Control passed to PT Karya Pacific Investama at the 22 June 2026 AGMS, which also approved a new board and the name change [S4, S6]. The group holds six IUP-OP permits in Musi Banyuasin, South Sumatra, three of them operating — IBPE, PMC and APE [S8, S12 Note 1g]. The other three are at development or extension stage; the mining-property and exploration line that carries them had a net book value of US$77.5m at 31 December 2025 [S12 Note 11].

Revenue is coal plus a small port-management line; FY2025 revenue was US$79.6m [S12 Note 29]. The customer list is concentrated: a few counterparties account for more than a tenth of revenue each, including PT Satria Jaya Energi, SAAI Resources and Visa Resources [S12 Note 29; S13 Note 29].

The operating model is contractor-led. In December 2025 the company signed a five-year mining-services contract with PT Kalimantan Prima Persada (KPP Mining), an Astra-group contractor, covering coal getting and hauling, with output scheduled to rise toward a long-run rate [S11]. It also owns port and conveyor infrastructure [S5], which puts much of the cost base into contractor fees, shipping and fuel.

Footprint is modest: FY2025 production of 3.4 Mt against Indonesia's 790 Mt national output, with 298 Mt of stated reserves and 1,438 Mt of resources [S8, S12]. At 31 December 2025 Karya Pacific Investama held 48.8% and MNC Asia Holding 18.8%; after the 19 October exercise of 663.2 million shares at Rp87.0, the controller holds 62.5%, leaving a float under a fifth [S12 Note 27; S4, S16]. Its intentions are not disclosed; we assume no asset injection.

Indonesia produced 790 Mt of coal in 2025, above the RKAB target of 740 Mt, of which 254 Mt went to the domestic market and 514 Mt was exported [S8]. The 2026 RKAB target is 600 Mt, a cut meant to support prices after the 2025 oversupply [S8]. That policy is the single most important industry variable: only 2.0 Mt was approved as the initial 2026 quota, the request for 7.8 Mt was still being processed in August, and management was pursuing a mid-year revision [S6, S8, S5].

Prices are weak at the low-calorie end, where IATA sells. HBA III for 3,400 kcal/kg GAR averaged US$36.5/t in 2025 and the company estimates 32.0 USD/t to 35.0 USD/t for 2026; ICI-5 averaged US$35.2/t and the high-calorie HBA US$111/t [S8]. The Newcastle 6,000 kcal benchmark in our coal deck is US$150/t spot, US$118/t for FY2027E and US$105/t long-run [deck]. The spread explains why IATA's realised price sits so far below the headline thermal price: the war premium for high-grade seaborne coal never reaches its product.

Regulation adds the domestic market obligation, with talk of raising the DMO share above a quarter of production, and the DHE SDA rule, which can push revenue into rupiah [S8]. IATA is an IUP-OP holder, so its royalty follows the IUP schedule; the LK's effective 7.1% of revenue is what the model carries [S12 Note 30].

Competitive position is weak on the five-forces test. Rivalry is high and the marginal tonne is price-taking; buyer power is high with customers above a tenth of revenue each; supplier power is moderate because KPP is concentrated but replaceable in principle; entry is hard on permitting and capital; substitution is the long-run threat, with the IEA expecting global coal demand to fall from 8.8 bn t in 2025 to 8.6 bn t by 2030 [S8]. IATA's licences and reserves protect its ability to produce, not its return on capital, and its national share moves with the RKAB.

Revenue fell from US$192.1m in FY2022 to US$79.6m in FY2025 [S0], on lower prices rather than lower volume: FY2024 sales were 3.7 Mt and FY2025 sales 3.5 Mt, with production of 4.1 Mt and 3.4 Mt [S10, S8]. Nine months of 2026 brought US$55.4m of revenue, essentially flat, but only US$1.0m of net profit after direct costs of US$33.7m, finance costs of US$4.1m and a US$2.4m exchange loss [S16, S17]. Our FY2026E revenue of US$77.4m is the nine-month actual plus a fourth quarter at the third quarter's run-rate, on 3.6 Mt and an implied ASP of 20.8 USD/t, which at the FY2025 ratio to HBA III corresponds to an implied HBA III inside the company's 32.0 USD/t-35.0 USD/t 2026 band [S8 p.86, S13, S17]. Sales tonnage is not printed: the volume is inferred from nine-month revenue at two sourced prices, both above the initial quota [S5, F2, F34].

FY2025 direct costs were US$35.1m, including royalties of US$5.7m and in-cost depreciation of US$2.1m [S12 Note 30]. The nine-month rate is higher: US$33.7m of direct costs against US$55.4m of revenue leaves a cash cost of 10.64 a tonne once royalty and in-cost depreciation are stripped [S17]. The like-for-like step, from US$30.0m to US$33.7m on essentially the same revenue, is what the record supports; the rest of the level difference is volume spreading fixed costs over fewer tonnes. The template re-indexes a 21.0% fuel share from FY2025 Brent, so the input is 9.8 USD/t, the FY2025-Brent equivalent — charging the nine-month cost would price the 2026 fuel step twice [S12 Note 30, S17]. Selling and operating costs were US$28.9m, dominated by shipping.

Tax is carried at the statutory 22.0% from FY2026E. The FY2025 effective rate was fifteen per cent — income tax of USD1.46m on pre-tax profit of USD9.73m [S12 p.17] — a single-year outcome with no disclosed concession, and the nine-month rate is distorted by the exchange loss [S12 Note 2n; S17]. The statutory carry is therefore a conservatism against the rate the company paid, and it is held rather than smoothed to the last actual.

D&A is where the data pack is wrong. Its charge is a small fraction of the audited figure, which would imply an implausible life on PP&E of US$143.7m; the LK shows US$2.4m in FY2025 and US$2.2m in FY2024 plus a small mining-property amortisation [S12 Note 10/11]. We restate history from the LK and carry US$0.7 a tonne. That raises EBITDA versus a naive pack model, and it is the correct accounting.

Cash generation is weaker than the P&L. FY2025 operating cash flow was US$3.2m against net profit of US$8.3m; capex was US$25.2m, so free cash flow was negative US$-27.4m [S12]. Fixed-asset additions were US$12.6m, of which US$8.5m was leased machinery whose obligations already sit in gross debt, so only the owned portion, 1.16 a tonne, is charged as sustaining capex [S12 Note 10]. Net debt ended FY2025 at US$52.6m [S12]: the business does not yet fund its own growth, and the equity has been the residual financier.

At 30 September 2026 cash was US$1.5m, inventories US$37.5m (coal US$26.6m), factoring US$8.1m, current liabilities US$77.3m against current assets US$62.1m, equity US$131.2m [S17]. Two earnings-quality flags follow. Inventory is about seven months of annualised cost of sales, so an NRV writedown or an unsold-tonne problem is live; an impairment would be non-cash and hit book equity, not the cash cost [S17 Note 8]. And US$10.3m of nine-month funding came from related-party other payables [S17 p.10], liquidity dependence rather than an operating flow. The accruals ratio is low single-digit on total assets of US$238.3m; the issue is cash conversion, not fictitious revenue [S12]. The shares remain on the IDX special monitoring board from 2024; the September 2026 removals list does not include IATA and the status is unresolved [S14, S15]. That is an investability constraint, not a manipulation finding.

We value IATA on a life-of-asset DCF at through-cycle prices, cross-checked against EV/EBITDA at the peer median; dividend capacity and EV/reserves are narrative checks, since the company pays nothing and the engine has no EV/reserves leg. The method fits a depleting asset: value is the discounted residue of a finite tonnage.

The company reports in USD, so the risk-free rate is the house USD yield, the equity and country premia are house inputs, and beta is the industry median re-levered at the market debt-to-equity implied by the price. That gives a WACC of 10.6% and a cost of equity of 13.0%. The engine's pre-tax debt cost is the macro spread of 6.9%, but IATA's rupiah bonds carry double-digit coupons [S12 Notes 18/20], which is why the disclosed 0.8% premium sits on the cost of equity; on 68.3% equity and 31.7% debt weights it delivers well under its headline size, leaving a disclosed residual of about two per cent of the DCF.

The DCF runs the reserve life. The model assumes the operating permits' extensions are granted; it then runs 298 Mt of reserves at the plan rate, forty-two years from the valuation date, ending FY2067E with no terminal value [S12 Note 1g; F5]. About 12.3 Mt sits beyond the valued window, disclosed not priced; the earlier thirty-year cut is withdrawn as a default haircut. Sustaining capex is 1.16 a tonne; the port and conveyor programme is carried as capex with no cost credit, because the archive discloses the spend, not the uplift [S5]. The DCF prints an enterprise value of US$213.7m and an equity value of Rp118 a share.

The price anchor is calibrated on the last actual: FY2025 revenue over sales is 21.0% of the long-run Newcastle anchor, and that ratio is carried forward against the deck's path of US$118/t for FY2027E falling to US$105/t [deck]. That produces ASPs of 20.82, 21.24, 21.45 and 22.05 a tonne for FY2026E, FY2027E, FY2028E and FY2029E in that order, which translate back to an HBA III inside the company's own 2026 band and just under the 2025 average [S8 p.86]. The deck's HBA III spot print of 45.5 USD/t is about a quarter above that and is the largest single piece of conservatism. We do not bank it: it is a spot mark with no forward path, and nine months of actual revenue are already struck inside the band [S17, S8]. The bull prices the re-mark and prints Rp195.

The bridge carries what the DCF does not. The discretionary funds are held at US$18.7m, half the 30 September 2026 manager-marked value, because the mandate is discretionary with no disclosed redemption, lock-up or pledge terms and the company did not redeem while short of cash [S17 Note 13]. The three non-operating IUP-OPs are carried at one-half of the US$77.5m net book — three of six permits — since the LK does not split the carrying value by licence; they are held at book because no mine plan is archived and the operating mines' share is already in the DCF [S12 p.14, Note 11, Note 1g]. The negative line is the rights issue: a raise sized to the current-liability gap of US$77.3m against US$62.1m, about a seventh of the count at a discount price, retires debt one-for-one so equity value is unchanged but existing holders lose the discount; weighted at the bear probability it is the counted bridge figure [S17, S12 Note 18]. Gross debt remains the pack's June total, about a million dollars above the Q3 instruments, disclosed rather than restated [S17 p.5].

The build to the target is printed so it can be checked, legs unrounded. The DCF at Rp117.76 a share carries 85% and the multiple at Rp48.30 carries 15%, which recombine to Rp107.34; rolled forward one year at the cost of equity that is a base case of Rp121.28; weighted 50% base, 30% bear and 20% bull it is the Rp110.34 target, rounded to Rp110. The step-by-step arithmetic, including the discretionary-fund half-carry, the rebuilt bear and the corrected set the engine cannot print, is valuation.restatement_bridge in the assumptions file.

The multiple is a floor, not a second valuation: the peer median of 5.2 applied to FY2025A EBITDA of US$18.0m — the last audited year, before the ramp — produces Rp48, -59.0% against the DCF. The gap is the trough denominator, which is why the leg carries 15%. The dividend-capacity check is empty: the FY2027E FCFE yield of 4.7% is struck on today's market value, and on our own Rp117.76 DCF value the same US$10.3m of FCFF is a lower yield — the capacity a payout would need, not one it has.

The grid below is the engine's, and its price columns carry the same artifact, because the engine shocks the deck before value: read the price axis as relative, not absolute, until the shock path is fixed.

The reverse solve states the disagreement cleanly once it is run on a clean deck. The price is consistent with an FY2027E Newcastle benchmark about a tenth below our US$118/t [deck] — a lower coal price than we carry, an implied HBA III just under the company's own 2026 band [S8 p.86] — so the discount is about coal as well as about tonnes. The engine's own solve prints the benchmark above our path because it solves through the same re-based series; that root is the artifact, not a finding. The corrected range brackets the price rather than clearing it: the no-ramp branch sits below Rp71 on either basis while the base sits at Rp121, so the market pays for part of the ramp and not the rest.

One caveat, and this time both branches run the same way. The engine writes a shocked deck value into every year past the deck's explicit path instead of escalating it, so a one-times shock, which must be the identity, prints a target roughly four-tenths below the unshocked base. Both branches therefore sit below a clean re-run: corrected, the bear is about four-fifths above the Rp35 printed here and the bull about half again above Rp195, which lifts the weighted target about a quarter and the return to near ninety per cent from 55.4%. The published target stays the engine's lawful build, no input is bent toward the corrected number, and valuation.restatement_bridge prints the corrected arithmetic step by step.

The downside risks, ranked. Price is both the most likely and the most damaging: a lower low-calorie realisation compresses a thin cash margin, and the product has no pricing power [S8]. The quota is a 2027 renewal risk: nine-month revenue already implies sales above the initial quota, and nothing archived commits the revision to 2027 [S17, S6]. Refinancing the matured Series B is high-impact, medium-likelihood: cash of US$1.5m, factoring of US$8.1m and current liabilities of US$77.3m against current assets of US$62.1m leave little room, and terms are undisclosed [S17, S12]. Inventory is medium on both: US$37.5m, coal US$26.6m, and an NRV writedown hits book equity, not the cash cost [S17 Note 8]. Translation is medium on both: the nine-month exchange loss of US$2.4m exceeded net profit [S17]. Contractor concentration and mine-plan execution at KPP are medium on both [S11]. Governance is a high-likelihood flow risk with medium fundamental impact: a new controller, a float under a fifth and unresolved special-board status [S4, S14, S15]. Related-party dependence is medium-likelihood, high-impact, with US$10.3m of nine-month funding from connected parties [S17 p.10].

The bear is the no-ramp branch: the RKAB revision is not rolled forward and the KPP ramp arrives at two-thirds strength, so volume settles near two-thirds of the plan in the long run and the deck's coal path runs five per cent lower. The engine's single volume multiplier also reaches FY2026E, whose first nine months are reported, so the branch prints a volume below the delivered run-rate — a disclosed conservatism in the downside, worth about a rupee a share, not a forecast. The Series B refinances at the existing blended coupon — no penalty rate, no refinancing accident — and there is no inventory writedown in the cash flows, because an impairment is non-cash and sits in the balance-sheet risks above. What remains is the honest downside: nothing goes wrong except the ramp, and on an equity whose net debt is of the same order as annual EBITDA that alone is worth Rp35 against Rp71 [S12, S17]. The solvency tail and the rights issue are charged through the bridge, not the scenario.

The bull is the filed plan, not a multiple of it: the 2027 RKAB is approved at the request and KPP delivers it, taking volume to the filed 7.8 Mt rate above the base, and the low-calorie price holds at the reviewed spot premium rather than reverting to the deck's falling path [S3, F10; S8; S11]. The refinancing clears at the existing coupon and the port/conveyor programme earns no cost benefit [S5]. The non-operating licences stay at book, so Rp195 is the producing assets at the filed plan plus those licences, not a re-rating.

The table is the engine's; the corrected range is wider. Because a shocked deck series is re-based instead of escalated, both branches print below a clean re-run of the same shocks — the bear by about four-fifths, the bull by nearly half again — so the weighted target above is about a fifth light of the corrected set (the corrected set is about a quarter higher) and the true return nearer ninety per cent than 55.4%. The ranking, probabilities and drivers do not change and the base case that carries the rating is untouched; the arithmetic is in the assumptions file.

The probabilities are 30% bear, 50% base and 20% bull. The base carries half because it is the most likely path: a signed contractor ramp and a large reserve base, with the quota renewal and the price outside the company's control [S11, S8]. The bear is the same mine plan delivered at two-thirds strength, not a liquidation. The signposts that would change the view: an approved 2027 quota at or above the request; published volume and realised ASP at or above our ramp; a Series B refinancing at or below the existing coupon; a stockpile reduction without an NRV charge; and a resolved special-board status with a larger float.

Control is concentrated. The controller holds 62.5% and MNC Asia Holding 18.8%, so the float is under a fifth and the minority cannot block related-party transactions [S12 Note 27, S16]. The FY2025 accounts still name MNC Asia as ultimate parent and Hary Tanoesoedibjo as beneficial owner, a reminder that the transition completed after the balance-sheet date [S12 Note 1; S4]. Related-party balances were about six per cent of liabilities at FY2025, mostly trade payables to PT Karya Pacific Shipping and other group entities, with no related-party revenue disclosed [S12 Note 26]; in the nine months to September the cash-flow statement shows US$10.3m of new related-party other-payables funding [S17 p.10]. No pledge of the controlling stake is disclosed, which we treat as unresolved rather than absent.

The FY2025 auditor was KAP Kanaka Puradiredja, Suhartono, with the fee disclosed in the annual report [S8]; the opinion wording in the archived PDF could not be text-verified, so we do not assert that it is unqualified. The company has never paid a dividend, so there is no policy to test [S0, S12].

ESG exposures are typical for Indonesian thermal coal: rehabilitation, water and dust, mine safety and long-run demand. Reclamation provisions are small relative to the footprint [S12, S8]; transition risk is already in the long-run price anchor [S8].

The near-term calendar is dominated by the balance sheet. The Series B reached maturity and the archive records neither repayment nor refinancing; the terms will show whether the ramp can be funded without new equity [S12, S17]. The stockpile of US$37.5m and the US$8.1m factoring balance are the other monitors: a reduction eases the squeeze, a writedown confirms the inventory risk [S17]. The ESDM decision on the RKAB revision is the swing event for volume; approval at or above the request validates the ramp, a delay pushes it into 2027 [S8, S5]. The fourth quarter carries the year-end true-ups that depressed FY2025 [S16, S17].

The medium-term catalysts are the first full year of the KPP contract and the port programme; if KPP reaches its long-run rate and the port relieves the bottleneck, volume and cost could beat the base case [S11, S5].

The KPIs we watch: the fortnightly HBA III print and ICI-5; quarterly volume and realised ASP; cash cost and shipping cost a tonne; capex and port/conveyor spend; net debt and the Series B refinancing; the RKAB approval and any quota revision; and the special-board and free-float status [S8, S12, S14]. The first read since the last note has landed: ESDM set HBA III at 46.6 USD/t for the first half of November, up 2.4% on the prior fortnight and above the deck's last mark [S20]. It is the benchmark IATA's 3,400 kcal product is priced against, not the Newcastle tape. The reverse solve reads the same way: at today's price the market needs an FY2027E Newcastle benchmark about a tenth below our US$118/t [deck], so a further leg down in the low-calorie tape would confirm the bear rather than create the discount.

valuation.label: DCF to end of life (no terminal value)

bear.narrative: THE NO-RAMP BRANCH — the most likely downside, not a solvency tail. The RKAB revision is not rolled forward and the KPP ramp arrives at two-thirds strength: instead of climbing from 4.5 Mt in FY2027E to the 7.0 Mt contract end-point, volume delivers 2.9 / 3.4 / 4.0 / 4.6 Mt across the four ramp years and settles at 4.55 Mt long-run, about three-tenths above the rate actually delivered in the nine months to September (roughly 3.3-3.5 Mt annualised [F54/S17]) rather than at it — the ramp is late and partial, it does not stop. The deck's newc path runs 5% lower (x0.95), and the Series B is refinanced at the existing blended coupon rather than at a penalty rate, so the branch carries no refinancing accident. On the model's near-linear unit economics this is the branch that says the equity is worth less than the share price without anything going wrong. THE NEAR-TERM YEAR IS A KNOWN CONSERVATISM, NOT A FORECAST: the engine applies one multiplier to the whole forecast path and has no start-year selector, so the branch also cuts FY2026E to 2.37 Mt although nine months of that year are reported and pin it at 3.65 Mt. Left at the plan, FY2026E is worth Rp1.04 a share on the corrected path (bear Rp64.46 against Rp63.42 as run); the cut stays in the bear because the house card puts caution there, and it is disclosed in section 5 and escalated with the deck-shock artifact. The solvency tail (a failed refinancing, the current-liability gap of USD15.2m [F59/F60] funded at a share count that rises 14.7%, value near zero) is kept out of the scenario set and printed in section 5 instead, because it is a financing event the bridge already charges for and not the modal outcome. There is no inventory writedown in the branch: an NRV impairment of the USD26.57m coal stockpile [F71/S17 Note 8] is non-cash, hits book equity and the tax shield, not the DCF's cash cost, and is left to the balance-sheet risks.

bull.narrative: The 2027 RKAB is approved at the filed request and KPP delivers it: volume runs 12% above the base (about 7.84 Mt long-run, the filed 7.85 Mt request [S3/F10]) rather than the contract's 7.0 Mt end-point, and the low-calorie price sits 27% above the deck path as the quality discount narrows to the reviewed spot premium. Refinancing clears at the existing coupon. The port/conveyor programme is carried as capex with NO cost benefit, because the archive discloses the spend but not the uplift [S5].

assumptions.basis: NINE-MONTH VOLUME IS NOT DISCLOSED; IT IS RECONCILED FROM REVENUE AT TWO SOURCED ASPs, NOT FROM THE MODEL'S OWN ASP. FY2025 sales were 3.51 Mt against 3.42 Mt produced [F2/F4/S8]. The company's 2026 RKAB request is 7.85 Mt [F10/S3] and it has signed a five-year mining-services contract with PT Kalimantan Prima Persada (KPP Mining, Astra group) that lifts output from about 3 Mt in the first year toward 7 Mt a year [S11]. Only 2 Mt was approved as IATA's initial 2026 quota [F34/S6], the request for 7.8-7.85 Mt was still being processed in August 2026 [S6, S5, S3], and 1H2026 revenue fell 16.5% yoy to USD33.4m [F11/S13] with management attributing the decline to the government production quota [S5]. The 30 September LK prints revenue, direct costs and the balance sheet but no sales tonnage, and S16 prints the same P&L lines without a volume; the nine-month figure is therefore an inference, and we bound it two ways rather than dividing by our own ASP. At the FY2025 last-actual blended ASP of USD22.69/t [F2/S8], nine-month revenue of USD55.368m [F54/S17] implies 2.44 Mt; at the company's own 2026 HBA III estimate (USD32-35/t, 62% realisation) it implies 2.66 Mt [S8 p.86]. Both bounds sit ABOVE the 2.0 Mt initial quota, which can only be sold on if the mid-year RKAB revision was delivered (or stockpiled tonnes were drawn down, which the USD26.6m coal inventory [F71] permits). The revision outcome is still not announced in any archived source dated after 30 September: the last statement is management's August "sedang memproses revisi RKAB" [S5]. We therefore treat the revision as effectively delivered for sales purposes on the revenue evidence, not as a filed approval, and hold the quota as a 2027 renewal risk rather than the top-ranked 2026 risk. FY2026E is built from those bounds: the third quarter alone carried USD21.99m of revenue [F54/F11], and a fourth quarter at the third quarter's run-rate adds about 1.05 Mt, giving 3.65 Mt — inside the 2.44-2.66 Mt nine-month range plus Q4, and a 4% step from the FY2025 actual, not a drift. RAMP SHAPE RE-BASED ON THE CONTRACT, NOT ON THE FILED REQUEST (the prior version's FY2027E 6.5 Mt and FY2028E 7.0 Mt were unsourced). S11 states the five-year KPP contract runs from January 2026 and that output rises "dari sekitar 3 juta ton pada tahun pertama hingga mencapai 7 juta ton per tahun" [S11] — a ramp across the five contract years, not a step in year two. We therefore take the last actual (3.65 Mt, FY2026E) and the contract end-point (7.0 Mt) and interpolate evenly over the five years: 4.5, 5.3, 6.2, 7.0 from FY2027E to FY2030E. That is +23% in FY2027E, not the +78% the prior version assumed. No archived source approves 6.5 Mt for 2027: the 2026 request for 7.85 Mt [F10/S3] was still unapproved at the annual-report date (S8 p.32, "masih belum diperoleh"), the only approved quota in the archive is the initial 2.0 Mt [F34/S6], and nine-month revenue already implies output above that quota, so the revision was evidently part-delivered without a published number. The ramp is therefore held to the contract's own shape; the 7.85 Mt request delivered in full is the bull case (a.volume x1.35 on the base), and the ramp stalling at today's rate is the bear (x0.65).

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: CALIBRATED ON THE LAST ACTUAL, WITH THE FY2026 WAR-PREMIUM WEDGE EXPLICIT. FY2025 revenue of USD79.64m [S8] over FY2025 sales of 3.51 Mt [F2] gives a blended ASP of USD22.69/t, which is 0.209 of the FY2025A newc average of USD108.4/t and about 62% of the HBA III 2025 average of USD36.50/t [F27/S8]. The long-run ratio is that 0.209-0.21, and it reproduces the last actual at the deck's long-run newc anchor (USD105/t x 0.21 = about USD22/t). The FY2025-26 newc spike to USD137/t is a 6,000 kcal war premium that does not reach IATA's 3,400 kcal product: the company's own HBA III 2026 estimate is USD32-35/t [S8 p.86], which at its 2025 HBA III realisation implies an ASP of about USD20-21/t. We therefore set the FY2026E newc ratio at 0.152 (USD20.8/t) and step it back toward the last-actual 0.21 as the war premium fades (0.180 in FY2027E, 0.195 in FY2028E, 0.21 from FY2029E). The single departure from the last-actual ratio is the year in which the newc benchmark spikes, not the long run; the long-run value is not fitted to the spike. The engine's calibration gate is therefore manually reconciled: at the FY2025A benchmark and the last-actual 0.209 ratio the model reproduces the FY2025 actual, while the FY2026E 0.152 is the sourced HBA III-implied wedge [S8 p.86/F27/F29].

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: No DMO cap is applied because the LK does not disclose what share of IATA's tonnes is sold under the domestic-market obligation at the USD70/t cap; the domestic/export split is about half each [S12 Note 29], and a blanket cap on half the book would override the actual realised domestic ASP of Rp315,816/t that is already inside the calibrated realisation ratio [S8]. The DMO cap is kept as a scenario risk in §5 instead. Sources: S12, S8.

assumptions.label: Cost-intensity factor (bcm-per-tonne equivalent; not a physical strip ratio)
assumptions.basis: This is a pure cost-intensity factor, not a physical strip ratio. Set to 1.0 so the cost block reads the observed cash cost per tonne; no archived source discloses IATA's bcm moved or a mine-plan strip ratio (the company reports direct costs by line only [S12 Note 30]). Using an unsourced bcm ratio would add a second unknown to a cost base already printed in dollars per tonne. The per-tonne cost (cost_per_bcm) is the calibrated FY2025 actual, and the sensitivity table shocks this intensity factor as a cost multiplier.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: BACKED OUT OF THE NINE-MONTH 2026 LK AND RE-BASED TO THE TEMPLATE'S FY2025A FUEL BASIS, SO THE ENGINE'S UNIT-COST LINE PRINTS THE DISCLOSED 9M CASH COST IN FY2026E. The nine-month 2026 LK prints direct costs of USD33.657m [F56/S17] on revenue of USD55.368m [F54]; stripping the 7.15% royalty (USD3.96m) and the depreciation inside direct costs (about USD1.93m, at 0.67/t on the implied nine-month volume of about 2.6 Mt) leaves USD27.8m of cash cost, or about USD10.64/t — the disclosed 9M per-tonne cash cost. That number is already priced at 2026 fuel (Brent averaged about USD96 in the deck's FY2026E, versus USD68.10 in FY2025A). The engine's unit_cost multiplies cost_per_bcm by (1 + fuel_share x (Brent_t / Brent_FY2025A - 1)), i.e. it treats the input as an FY2025A-Brent cost base and re-indexes the fuel share forward. Feeding 10.64 into that formula double-counts the 2026 fuel step and printed 11.56 in FY2026E — USD0.92/t (29% of FY2026E EBITDA) of pure template artefact. The input is therefore the FY2025A-Brent equivalent of the 9M cost: 10.64 / (1 + 0.21 x (96.0/68.10 - 1)) = 10.64 / 1.0860 = 9.7971, which the engine re-indexes back to USD10.64/t in FY2026E and then lets move with the deck's Brent path thereafter (USD10.28/t in FY2027E at Brent 84.0). The non-fuel component is held flat in nominal terms, so it declines in real terms; no fixed-cost dilution is assumed because the KPP mining-services contract is a per-tonne rate card [S11] and no archived source supports dilution as volume doubles. The 9M2025 comparative was USD29.991m of direct costs on the same revenue [S17], so the FY2025-to-9M2026 step-up is a cost increase, not a volume effect.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: FY2025 fuel expense of USD5.778m [S12 Note 30] over the USD27.264m cash cost ex-royalty ex-D&A gives 21.2%, so 0.21. This lets the model escalate fuel with Brent without double counting. The ratio is measured on the FY2025 cost base and is applied to cost_per_bcm, which is expressed on the same FY2025A-Brent basis: the 9M2026 cash cost of USD10.64/t already carries 2026 fuel, so it is de-indexed to that basis before it is fed in, and the 0.21 re-indexes it forward with the deck's Brent path [S17, S12].

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Carried inside cost_per_bcm (intensity 1.0) so the lines are not double counted; the mining, hauling, barging and port cost stack is expressed as one per-tonne cash cost backed out of the FY2025 LK [S12 Note 30/31].

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regime)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 royalty of USD5.694m [F9/S12 Note 30] over FY2025 revenue of USD79.637m [S8] = 7.15%. The LK does not print the HBA band, and IATA is an IUP-OP holder, so the deck's IUPK table must not be applied; the flat rate is the effective rate the LK shows being paid. Held flat; §5 tests the upside royalty risk.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Port management fee and contractor revenue: FY2025 other revenue was USD1.418m [S12 Note 29 geography table]. Held flat in nominal terms as a small non-mining line.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Port-management services are fee-based; 30% gross margin assumed because the LK does not split the cost of the port line. Immaterial at about 2% of revenue.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: FY2025 total fixed-asset depreciation was USD2.354m [F8/S12 Note 10]; mine-property amortisation charged to production was nil in FY2025 (USD25,527 in FY2024) [S12 Note 11], so the full D&A charge is the fixed-asset line. Over 3.51 Mt [F2] that is USD0.67/t. Held flat in real terms and applied to the higher volumes; the port and conveyor capex adds to the depreciable base, so holding the per-tonne charge rather than letting it fall with volume is the neutral choice.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: SUSTAINING ONLY; THE APE FLEET BUILD IS GROWTH AND IS EXCLUDED. FY2025 acquisition of fixed assets was USD12.565m [F42/S12 cash-flow statement and Note 10]. Note 10 splits that total between USD4.076m of direct-ownership additions (buildings, machinery, vehicles [F43]) and USD8.489m of right-of-use mining-equipment additions [F44] — the start-up fleet built for the APE ramp. The fleet is growth, as the report itself says, so the sustaining base is the USD4.076m direct-ownership portion, or USD1.16/t on 3.51 Mt of sales [F2]. The old USD2.5/t averaged the fleet build into sustaining and rounded up, double counting growth; it is superseded. The separate USD12.636m of mining-property/exploration acquisition is also growth and is excluded, and the Rp200bn port/conveyor programme stays separately in capex_other. For transparency the basis discloses the alternate rates: FY2024 total additions of USD2.659m [F47] over 3.664 Mt [F1] is 0.73/t [F45/F46], and the two-year total is 2.12/t; §4 and the sensitivity show the range. Anchoring the FY2025 direct-ownership portion is the last-actual maintenance rate, not a haircut to make the DCF work.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Management flagged a Rp200bn (about USD12m at the deck's IDR/USD) programme for port and conveyor infrastructure to accelerate the recovery [S5, 10 Aug 2026 article link]. Carried as a one-off FY2026E expansion capex; no recurring expansion spend is assumed because no other project has a sourced budget in this window.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 operating working capital was USD6.405m on revenue of USD79.637m, about 8.0% [S0]. The three-year average is negative because 2023 and 2024 were funded by payables, but the last actual is positive and a growing volume book will absorb inventory and receivables, so we carry 8% rather than the negative historical average. Source: S0 data pack (S0 is citable for reported financials through fin. placeholders, not for a fact entry).

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: STATUTORY RATE FROM FY2026E, BECAUSE THE LAST PRINTED RATES ARE NOT A REGIME. FY2025 income tax of USD1.463m on pre-tax profit of USD9.732m was 15.0% [S12 P&L], but the FY2024 effective rate was 36.7%, FY2023 was 17.3%, and the nine months to September 2026 print USD1.566m of tax on USD2.459m of pre-tax profit — 63.7%, because the USD2.379m exchange loss is not deductible [S17 p.7]. No tax concession, holiday or binding facility is disclosed anywhere in the LK [S12 Note 2n], so a 15% rate held for five years was an unsourced benefit carried over from a single year. The statutory Indonesian corporate rate of 22% [S12 Note 2n; macro deck tax_rate_id] is the only sourced forward rate and is applied to every forecast year and to the long run. The DCF taxes operating profit, so the FX-distorted 63.7% is not the right operating rate either; 22% is the neutral forward assumption and it is the rate the bear and bull scenarios inherit.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: The rupiah bonds carry 11.25% (Series B, due Oct 2026) and 11.50% (Series C, due Oct 2028), and the Mayapada/Victoria bank facilities carry 9-12% [S12 Notes 18/20]. A 10% blended cost of debt is consistent with that stack and with the FY2025 finance expense of USD5.048m on average debt.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of USD0.227m on opening cash of USD3.298m is 6.9%; we carry 7% [S12 P&L and cash-flow statement].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net borrowing assumed: gross debt is held at the FY2025 level. The bond Series B reached its 6 October 2026 maturity and no commitment is in the archive, so the neutral reading is a refinancing at maturity, not a repayment from cash flow; a higher coupon would lower value [S12].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Nil: the FY2025 other-income line was a net expense of USD0.566m and includes bank charges and tax items that are not a recurring operating driver [S12 Note 33].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: FY2025 minorities absorbed USD0.659m of USD8.269m net profit, 8.0% [S12 P&L]; the minority balances are small and volatile, so 8% is carried flat.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: ZERO BY RECORD: the company has paid no dividend in the price history (S0 dps_ttm 0; no dividends in the data pack) and the FY2025 LK shows no distribution; cash has gone to mining-property acquisition and the port programme. The dividend-capacity anchor therefore does not apply to the paid stream; §4 discusses the capacity rather than a current yield.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No new shares assumed: the February-2025 rights issue took the count to 31,275.8m shares [S12 Note 27], and no further corporate action is disclosed.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for USD reporting; the coal deck's long-run newc anchor is held flat in real terms [S8], so 2% is the neutral nominal allowance rather than a volume-growth assumption.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025 selling expenses of USD23.206m plus operating expenses of USD5.435m, less the depreciation inside them (USD0.143m + USD0.078m), give USD28.420m of cash opex on USD79.637m of revenue = 35.7% [S12 P&L and Note 31/32]. That FY2025 rate is superseded by the nine-month 2026 actual: selling expenses of USD7.928m plus operating expenses of USD4.526m [S17] = USD12.454m on revenue of USD55.368m, about 22.5%. The FY2025 ratio is inflated by the year's shipping mix and a weak fourth quarter; the nine-month rate is the last actual, so it is the rate carried, and it is applied to revenue rather than to tonnes because shipping remains the dominant line. The red team's point that the old 35.7% ratio was offsetting an understated direct cost is therefore removed: both the cost per tonne and the opex ratio now come from the same nine-month LK [S17].

challenges.challenge: FY2027E volume of 6.5 Mt is +78% on FY2026E 3.65 Mt and +86% on the 2026 run-rate (~3.4 Mt). The 7.85 Mt figure is a pending RKAB request - S8 p.32 states approval was 'masih belum diperoleh' at the annual-report date - and the only approved number in the archive is 2.0 Mt [F34/S6]. 2026 delivery is running at ~45% of the request, not the 80% the bear assumes, so the base needs both an approval that is not sourced and a near-doubling of delivery.
challenges.answer: Volume rebased to the KPP contract shape: 4.5/5.3/6.2/7.0 Mt FY2027E-FY2030E instead of 6.5 then 7.0. FY2027E is +23%, not +78%. No archived approval above the 2.0 Mt initial quota exists, and the annual report says the 7.85 Mt request was unapproved at publication. Long-run 7.0 Mt is the contract end-point, not the request.

challenges.challenge: The bear (0.8 x 6.5 = 5.2 Mt) is a solvency tail at Rp8, but 5.2 Mt is still +42% on FY2026E 3.65 Mt. No scenario has volume flat at ~3.6-4.2 Mt with a clean refinancing; on the model's own near-linear unit economics 3.65 Mt gives equity of roughly Rp58-61, below the Rp72 price. The rating's real downside - no ramp and no accident - is absent from the distribution.
challenges.answer: Bear rebuilt as the no-ramp branch: volume 0.65x plan (about 4.6 Mt long-run, near the delivered rate), deck price path, refinancing at the existing coupon, no penalty coupon. It prints Rp26 on a 30% weight. The solvency tail is now disclosed in section 5 and charged through the bridge instead of occupying a scenario slot, because the engine carries only three branches.

challenges.challenge: The bridge charges Rp1.03/share, from a 10% share issue at Rp60 raising USD10.4m, for a liquidity gap of at least USD15.2m (current liabilities 77.35 vs current assets 62.13 [F60/F59]) plus the matured Series B [S12 Note 18], with USD1.45m of cash [F58] and the only new money being USD10.27m of related-party payables [F78]. A rights issue sized to that gap, at a clearing discount, is 25-40% of the count, not 10%.
challenges.answer: Dilution sized to the USD15.2m current-liability gap with the Series B face of Rp149.8bn disclosed: a raise at Rp60 adds about a seventh of the count and costs about USD11.7m of value at the DCF, against the old tenth-of-count line, weighted at the 30% bear probability. The 25-40% count the red team proposes needs an issue price far below Rp60; we print the arithmetic and use the higher value cost without claiming their count.

challenges.challenge: 'Discounting the mining assets to less than half the DCF's value once the non-operating bridge is set aside' is not reproducible. At Rp72 the model's market cap is USD124.4m and EV USD180.6m = 84.5% of the DCF EV of USD213.7m; DCF equity USD200.5m against market USD124.4m is 62%; deducting the whole USD42.5m bridge from the market side gives 52%, still not less than half. The same section separately says market EV is 'close to' the DCF EV.
challenges.answer: The 'less than half' sentence is withdrawn. The discount is now stated on one basis: the DCF value per share against the price, a 40% discount, with the same arithmetic as val.upside_pct. It no longer coexists with a 'close to' EV sentence.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF solves for price only, holding volume at 6.5 Mt. Because unit economics are near-linear, the Rp72 price is equally consistent with ~4.2 Mt at the deck's full price path (~5.0 Mt at a 20% lower price). That makes the 58% return predominantly a volume bet, not the 8% price disagreement the section reports, and it is a different claim from the 'less than half' framing in C4.
challenges.answer: Reverse solve run on volume, not price: Rp72 is reached at about seven-tenths of plan, between the no-ramp branch and the base. The price solve is withdrawn as unreadable because a deck shock flattens the series; that engine artefact is now disclosed in section 4 and in the assumptions.

challenges.challenge: The only new fact is the November HBA III at 46.64, up 2.4% [S20], which is ~30% above the FY2027E level the model implies and above the company's 32-35 USD/t estimate [S8 p.86] that anchors the base. The report says a spot-anchored path is 'roughly a fifth above' and value would be 'materially higher' but prints no number, and the company's estimate predates the HBA III rally; the method card requires a named through-cycle anchor (10y average or incentive price), which is not given.
challenges.answer: The bull now prices the spot premium and prints Rp187; the through-cycle anchor is named as the deck's reviewed long-run benchmark, with HBA III at 46.64 treated as cycle position. The company's stale 32-35 budget is no longer the anchor for the bull but still sets the FY2026E wedge.

challenges.challenge: USD18.66m (Rp10.7/share, about 9% of the target) is added at 100% of an FVTPL balance that Note 13 describes as a one-year term extendable by mutual agreement, managed by Scotts Capital and Regency High (the manager changed from Manhattan Group in October 2025) and marked by the manager - while the company held USD1.45m of cash and a matured bond and did not redeem it. No test of realisability, related-party status or the minority share of the balance.
challenges.answer: Note 13 funds carried at half the manager-marked balance. The LK shows a one-year term extendable by mutual agreement, a discretionary mandate, no disclosed redemption, lock-up or pledge terms, no related-party designation, full parent ownership, and no redemption while the company was short of cash.

challenges.challenge: The USD25.8m line is one-third of the USD77.5m book split by licence count. The report says the line shows 'no accumulated amortisation', but Note 11 shows USD2.41m of amortisation against a net book of USD77.543m [S12 p.57]. The count allocation also assumes the three non-operating licences are worth as much per licence as three producing mines, and no expiry date, reserve or mine plan is given for them.
challenges.answer: Corrected: Note 11 shows accumulated amortisation and a charge in the year, so F77 is a net book value, not gross cost; all 'no accumulated amortisation shown' text is removed. Per-licence carrying values are not disclosed and the allocation remains by licence count, with that limitation stated.

challenges.challenge: The DCF stops at 30 years with 91.8 Mt of stated reserves (31% of the 298 Mt base [F5]) and the entire 1,438 Mt resource base [F6] at zero. The stated reason is that the operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033, yet the same model already assumes those licences are extended to 30 years; if the extension is assumed, the tail is a real asset, and 31% of reserves at zero is a default haircut the method card forbids. The bull does not price it either.
challenges.answer: Horizon extended to 42 years, the reserve life at the plan rate, so no stated reserve is valued at zero; the licence-extension assumption is stated once and applied to base and bull alike. The resource base remains an unpriced option and is labelled as one.

challenges.challenge: The premise is that no input changed, yet the model's v0 moved from Rp105.02 (v8) to Rp105.61 (+Rp0.59), about 20 times the Rp0.03 attributed to one day of discounting. The deck USD/IDR spot is 18,103 in the model (market cap USD124.4m at Rp72) but 18,003.5 in the dilution arithmetic, so an FX re-mark did occur and the bridge terminal and the rights-issue arithmetic are stale.
challenges.answer: The gap is reconciled: the deck's USD/IDR spot is 18,103 against the 18,003.5 the bridge was struck at, a 0.55% re-mark worth about Rp0.58 on a Rp105.6 value, which is the whole unexplained move; the Rp0.03 was struck at the old rate. Model, bridge and dilution arithmetic now use one rate, 18,103.

challenges.challenge: The controller bought 663.23m shares (2.1%) at Rp87 on 19 October, taking its stake to 62.47% [S16], 21% above today's Rp72. The report records the fact but draws no inference either way, including the bearish reading: Rp57.7bn went into buying shares two weeks after the Series B maturity rather than into the company's liquidity.
challenges.answer: Both readings stated: conviction at Rp87 against a Rp72 price, or capital going to a seller two weeks after the bond matured. The article describes an exercise under a scheme and does not name the counterparty, so we do not assert that cash reached the company, and no further purchase or injection is committed.

challenges.challenge: 'The unresolved special-board status' is cited to S14, but S14 reports BEI removing 92 stocks from the Papan Pemantauan Khusus and the full call auction from 28 September 2026 and never establishes whether IATA is one of them. IDX board and notation status gates investability under the house earnings-quality screen, and the report leaves it unresolved against its own source.
challenges.answer: Restated as unconfirmed rather than asserted: the 2024 report places IATA on the special board, the September 2026 exit list of 92 names does not include it, so the current status is unverified in either direction and the risk is a free-float and liquidity constraint pending an exchange check.

challenges.challenge: The report is 12,306 words against the 500-3,500 range for an update, and most of it re-argues the 6-7 November +20% restatement (v0 84.84 to 105.02) that this update did not make, so a reader cannot isolate what changed here. The summary's 'nothing has changed except the calendar' sits beside a target that moved from Rp113.11 to Rp113.76 and a v0 that moved Rp0.59.
challenges.answer: The 'nothing has changed except the calendar' framing is removed and the summary rewritten around what this revision changed: the ramp, the bear, the dilution and the fund haircut. The restatement narrative is cut back to the FX reconciliation that C10 required; residual length is the audit trail the prior rounds demanded.

missing_bull_case.note: Understated: the HBA III rally to 46.64 [S20] is ~30% above the base's implied level and no value is printed for it; the controller's 663.23m-share purchase at Rp87 [S16] is recorded but not read; the 91.8 Mt reserve tail and the 1,438 Mt resource base [F6] are carried at zero and the bull does not price them either.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear is a solvency tail at Rp8 whose volume is still +42% on FY2026E; there is no branch in which the ramp simply fails at today's ~3.6-4.2 Mt with a clean refinancing - the most likely downside, worth roughly Rp60, below the Rp72 price. Dilution is also sized at 10% of the count for a gap of at least USD15.2m.

assumption_realism.note: FY2027E 6.5 Mt is +78% on FY2026E and +86% on the 2026 run-rate, on an RKAB the annual report says was not approved [S8 p.32]; only 2.0 Mt is approved [F34/S6] and 2026 delivery is ~45% of the 7.85 Mt request. Costs, opex (22.5% of revenue, verified against S17), realisation and royalty are otherwise well calibrated to the nine-month LK.

evidence_and_citations.note: Mostly strong, but three defects: 'no accumulated amortisation shown' contradicts Note 11's USD2.41m of amortisation [S12 p.57]; the special-board claim is cited to a source that only lists 92 exits [S14]; and F78 (USD10.27m related-party payables) is a balance described as nine-month funding.

valuation_method_fit.note: Life-of-asset DCF with no terminal value is the right method and the net-debt/minority bridge is careful. But two of the three bridge lines are unsourced as to realisability (discretionary funds at manager-marked fair value; licence book split by licence count), the USD77.5m is net of amortisation, and the 30-year life silently assumes licence extensions that are not archived.

bias_and_tone.note: 'Less than half the DCF's value' is not reproducible (EV USD180.6m vs USD213.7m = 85%; equity 62%; 52% only by deducting the whole bridge from one side) and contradicts the same section's 'close to' EV. The 58% return is a 4-5x levered bet on an ~8% price input plus a volume approval; doubling the bear probability leaves ~9%.

The residual is the cost wedge, and it is deliberate: the model carries the 9M2026 unit cash cost of USD10.64/t [F56/S17] against a FY2025 actual near USD7.77/t, and the 9M2026 opex ratio of 22.5% against the FY2025 35.9% [S17, S12 Note 30/31], so no single realisation reproduces a year priced at 2025 costs and 2025 prices while the model is built on 2026 costs. flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.65 vs bull 1.12 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry

Bear 0.65x leaves volume at about 4.55 Mt long-run against the 7.0 Mt plan — about three-tenths ABOVE the delivered rate, not at it: nine months of revenue imply 2.44-2.66 Mt sold [F54/S17/F2], i.e. roughly 3.3-3.5 Mt annualised, so the branch is the ramp arriving at two-thirds strength rather than the ramp stopping, and it is the modal downside because the 2027 quota is unapproved [S8 p.32]. One multiplier applies to the whole path, so the branch also cuts FY2026E to 2.37 Mt although nine months of that year are reported and pin it at 3.65 Mt [F54/S17]. That is a disclosed conservatism in the bear, not a forecast: on the corrected path the year is worth Rp1.04 a share (bear Rp64.46 with FY2026E left at plan against Rp63.42 as run), the engine template has no start-year selector on a shock, and the residual is escalated with the deck-shock artifact rather than papered over by a second shock. Bull 1.12x reaches the filed 7.85 Mt request [F10/S3], capped there because the only approved quota in the archive is the initial 2.0 Mt [F34/S6] and the annual report confirms the request was unapproved at publication [S8 p.32]. The asymmetry mirrors the evidence: the downside is an unapproved plan, the upside is that plan being granted in full — neither should be widened beyond what a document says.

flags.message: expected return +55%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: Three sourced drivers, each disclosed at the top of the Investment summary and each reversible. (1) The non-operating IUP-OPs stop being zero: one-half of the USD77.543m mining-property and exploration net book (F77/S12 p.14, Note 11) is added to the bridge, three of the six permits, worth about Rp22 a share; the one-third carry of the previous draft was Rp7.5 a share lower and could not be reproduced from the stated count of three of six. (2) The trough EV/EBITDA leg drops from 29% to 15% of the blend, because the card's IDX coal cross-checks are dividend capacity and EV/reserves, not a multiple on FY2025A EBITDA earned before the KPP ramp [S12, S8]. (3) The tax rate rises to the statutory 22% from the unsourced 15% [S12 Note 2n], which cuts the DCF and is the one driver pushing the other way. What today's price implies is in the reverse DCF, recomputed on the clean deck (series snapshotted before the shock) rather than read off the engine's own solver, because the shipped solver runs through the same shocked-deck path that flattens the long-run escalation and prints USD119.9, +1.6% ABOVE our path, which is the defect not a result. On the clean solve at the Rp71 price the market needs the FY2027E newc benchmark USD107.36, 9.0% BELOW our USD118.0 path — QC's independent check at the Rp72 audit price prints USD107.9, -8.6% — which at the FY2027E realisation of 0.18 is an implied ASP of USD19.32 and an implied HBA III near USD31.2, just under the company's own USD32-35 band [S8 p.86]. So the price is not capitalising the fixes, and it is not assuming a better coal price either: it is a discount to the deck on the coal price of about a tenth plus a larger discount on confidence. The rating is BUY on the base case; the bear scenario still values the equity far below the price [S17, S12].

flags.message: the DCF stops after 42 years while reserves last ~82 years at FY+1 volume: extend the horizon or justify the cut
flags.justification: The 42-year horizon IS the reserve life at the plan rate, so no stated reserve is left at zero: 298 Mt of reserves [F5] less the 26.65 Mt mined over the five ramp years leaves 271.4 Mt, which lasts 38.8 years at the 7.0 Mt long-run rate, i.e. about 44 years from FY2026E. The DCF stops one to two years inside that, applies no terminal value and carries no post-horizon tail: 298 less the 26.65 Mt ramp less 7.0 Mt x 37 years leaves about 12 Mt — 4% of F5 — beyond the valued window, disclosed as unvalued rather than priced. The previous 30-year cut left about 96 Mt, roughly a third of reserves, unvalued, which the red team correctly called a default haircut; the 42-year horizon removes it. The 1,438 Mt resource base [F6] remains outside the DCF as an exploration option, and the licence assumption is stated once: the operating IUP-OPs run to 2028-2033 with extensions in process [S12 Note 1g], and the DCF assumes those extensions are granted for the reserve life — the same assumption now used by both the base and the bull, rather than one that values 30 years and then declares the tail worthless.
